title: Average Value of a Function and Net Change
subject: AP Calculus AB

chunks.text: The average value of a continuous function f on [a, b] is f_avg = (1/(b − a))∫ from a to b of f(x) dx.
The average value formula is the continuous version of 'sum divided by count': the integral sums the values and (b − a) plays the role of the count.
Geometrically, the average value is the height of a rectangle of width (b − a) that has the same area as the region under the curve.
The average value carries the units of f itself (a height), not the units of a rate.
Example: the average value of f(x) = x² on [0, 3] is (1/3)∫₀³ x² dx = (1/3)(9) = 3.
A common error is computing the integral and forgetting to divide by the interval length (b − a).
Average value of a function differs from average rate of change: average value (1/(b−a))∫f dx is a height, while average rate of change [f(b) − f(a)]/(b − a) is a slope.
The Net Change Theorem states that ∫ from a to b of f'(x) dx = f(b) − f(a).
The Net Change Theorem means integrating a rate of change over an interval gives the net change in the quantity.
A final amount equals the initial amount plus the accumulated change: f(b) = f(a) + ∫ from a to b of f'(x) dx.
Given a rate function and a starting value, integrate the rate to find how much is added or removed, then add to the start for the final amount.
Because the integral is signed, a rate that is sometimes positive and sometimes negative automatically yields the net change.
Example: water flowing at r(t) = 3t L/min for 0 ≤ t ≤ 4 adds ∫₀⁴ 3t dt = 24 liters.
If the tank in that example starts with 10 liters, it holds 10 + 24 = 34 liters at t = 4.
The units of the net-change integral are (rate units)·(time units), which cancel to give the quantity's units.
On free response, 'how much was added or used' is the net-change integral alone, while 'how much is present at the end' is the initial value plus that integral.
The Mean Value Theorem for Integrals states that a continuous function on [a, b] attains its average value f(c) = f_avg at some c in [a, b].
In the equal-area picture, the Mean Value Theorem for Integrals point is where the curve crosses the horizontal average-value line.
The Mean Value Theorem for Integrals is the integral analog of the ordinary Mean Value Theorem, which guarantees a tangent slope equal to the average slope.
The Mean Value Theorem for Integrals confirms that the average value is a genuine representative value the function actually reaches.
Average value is used wherever a continuously varying quantity needs a single representative number, such as average temperature, velocity, or concentration.
The two key ideas of the lesson are average value (a representative height) and net change (the integral of a rate), both built on the definite integral.
